passages.text: Genotypic and Phenotypic Analysis in Chinese Cohort With Autosomal Recessive Osteogenesis Imperfecta

Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) is a rare heritable skeletal disorder which is mainly caused by defected type I collagen. <sentence_start/>Autosomal recessive OI (AR-OI) is caused by mutations of genes that are responsible for type I collagen modification and folding, and is often associated with more severe phenotypes. <sentence_start/>Due to the limited number of recessive OI patients, it has been difficult to study the mutation spectrum as well as the correlation of genotype and phenotype. <sentence_start/>This study recruited a Chinese cohort of 74 AR-OI families, aiming to establish the mutation spectrum and to examine the genotypic and phenotypic correlation. <sentence_start/>We identified 82 variants including 25 novel variants and 57 HGMD reported variants in these AR-OI patients, using whole exome sequencing/panel sequencing combined with Sanger sequencing. <sentence_start/>Pathogenic mutations were found at <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 30, 40.54%), <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 22, 29.73%), <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 10, 13.51%), <italic toggle="yes">CRTAP</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3, 4.05%), <italic toggle="yes">P3H1</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3, 4.05%), <italic toggle="yes">SERPINH1</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 2, 2.70%), <italic toggle="yes">SEC24D</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3, 4.05%), and <italic toggle="yes">PLOD2</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 1, 1.35%) respectively. <sentence_start/>Thus, <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> represents the most frequent pathogenic gene of AR-OI in Chinese population. <sentence_start/>The most common clinical manifestations of AR-OI patients include walking problem (72.86%), scoliosis (65.28%) and frequent fractures (fractures ≥2/year) (54.05%). <sentence_start/>Interestingly, ptosis represents a unique phenotype of patients carrying <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> variants, and it was rare in patients harboring other pathogenic genes. <sentence_start/>Our study expanded the mutation spectrum of AR-OI and enriched the knowledge of genotypic and phenotypic correlation in Chinese cohort with AR-OI.
Introduction

Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI), also known as brittle bone disease, is a genetically and clinically heterogeneous skeletal disorder. <sentence_start/>Typical clinical manifestations include low bone mass, frequent fractures, short stature, blue sclerea, and bone deformity. <sentence_start/>More than 90% of OI cases are caused by a defect of type I collagen, and therefore OI is known as an autosomal dominant inherited disease due to a mutation in <italic toggle="yes">COL1A1</italic> or <italic toggle="yes">COL1A2</italic>, which encodes alpha 1 or alpha 2 chains of type I collagen (<citation rid="B20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.20429" pmid="17078022" pmcid="PMC4144349" count="1">Marini et al., 2007</citation>). <sentence_start/>Multiple genes have been reported to contribute to the development of autosomal recessive OI (AR-OI), including <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">LEPRE1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">CRTAP</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PPIB</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">BMP1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">SP7</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PLOD2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">TMEM38B</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">P4HB</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">SERPINH1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">SEC24D</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">CREB3L1</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">SPARC</italic> (<citation rid="B9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.trsl.2016.11.005" pmid="27914223" count="1">Kang et al., 2017</citation>). <sentence_start/>Although the incidence rate of AR-OI is < 10% of the whole OI population, the clinical manifestations of AR-OI are much more severe than the dominant OI patients (<citation rid="B16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00198-017-4143-4148" pmid="28725987" count="1">Liu et al., 2017</citation>; <citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.23718" pmid="30715774" count="1">Li et al., 2019</citation>).

Synthesis of type I collagen is a sophisticated process. <sentence_start/>With the development of next generation sequencing, remarkable progress has been made in identifying new genes associated with the modification and folding of type I collagen. <sentence_start/>These genes have formed a unique biological network, and deficiency in any individual gene may lead to recessive OI. <sentence_start/>Propeptides encoded by <italic toggle="yes">COL1A1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">COL1A2</italic> undergo post-translational modifications in the endoplasmic reticulum, followed by transportation to Golgi and cleavage of N-/C- terminal propeptides. <sentence_start/>Consequently, collagen fibers are formed to further build up the collagen matrix. <sentence_start/>Defect in any step during the type I collagen synthesis can lead to the development of OI (<citation rid="B9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.trsl.2016.11.005" pmid="27914223" count="1">Kang et al., 2017</citation>). <sentence_start/>For example, deficiency of <italic toggle="yes">CRTAP</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">P3H1</italic> or <italic toggle="yes">PPIB</italic>, the components of collagen prolyl 3-hydroxylation complex, will lead to defects in post translational modification of unfolded collagen alpha-chains (<citation rid="B21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2006.08.039" pmid="17055431" count="1">Morello et al., 2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>Mutations in <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">SERPINH1</italic> or <italic toggle="yes">BMP1</italic> cause defects in collagen folding and crosslinking (<citation rid="B12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.M601369200" pmid="16484215" count="1">Koide et al., 2006</citation>; <citation rid="B27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/hmg/dds371" pmid="22949511" pmcid="PMC3606010" count="1">Schwarze et al., 2013</citation>; <citation rid="B9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.trsl.2016.11.005" pmid="27914223" count="1">Kang et al., 2017</citation>). <sentence_start/>Alterations in <italic toggle="yes">SP7</italic> (<citation rid="B3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ydbio.2017.09.010" pmid="28899668" count="1">Azetsu et al., 2017</citation>), <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> (<citation rid="B11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2013.02.010" pmid="23499309" pmcid="PMC3617378" count="1">Keupp et al., 2013</citation>; <citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/NEJMoa1215458" pmid="23656646" pmcid="PMC3709450" count="1">Laine et al., 2013</citation>; <citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2013.02.009" pmid="23499310" pmcid="PMC3617391" count="1">Pyott et al., 2013</citation>) or <italic toggle="yes">CREB3L1</italic> (<citation rid="B23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncb1963" pmid="19767743" count="1">Murakami et al., 2009</citation>) affect osteoblast differentiation (<citation rid="B7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s0140-6736(15)00728-x" pmid="26542481" pmcid="PMC7384887" count="1">Forlino and Marini, 2016</citation>). <sentence_start/>Dysfunction of PEDF, which is encoded by <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic>, will damage the bone homeostasis (<citation rid="B1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bbrc.2009.11.139" pmid="19945427" count="1">Akiyama et al., 2010</citation>).

Although mutation spectrums on autosomal dominant OI have been established in large cohorts of Chinese (<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.23718" pmid="30715774" count="1">Li et al., 2019</citation>), Swedish (<citation rid="B15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ejhg.2015.81" pmid="25944380" pmcid="PMC4795106" count="1">Lindahl et al., 2015</citation>) and Canadian/American populations (<citation rid="B4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00198-016-3709-3701" pmid="27509835" count="1">Bardai et al., 2016</citation>), mutation spectrum on AR-OI remains unclear due to its rare incidence. <sentence_start/>There was only one report about the molecular spectrum based on findings from a small cohort of 19 recessive OI patients from Mediterranean (<citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1359/jbmr.091109" pmid="19929435" count="1">Rauch et al., 2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>Here, we examined the mutation spectrum in 74 AR-OI families, the largest cohort worldwide to our knowledge. <sentence_start/>Current findings expand our knowledge about the gene spectrum and phenotypic spectrum of AR-OI, and provide important information for genetic diagnosis of AR-OI patients.
Materials and Methods
Subjects

We recruited 74 AR-OI probands from a cohort of 1095 OI patients (646 families) in mainland China. <sentence_start/>These patients displayed typical clinical manifestations of OI: recurrent fractures, short stature, bone malformation, with or without extra-skeletal manifestations such as blue sclera, hearing loss and dentinogenesis imperfecta. <sentence_start/>After obtaining approval from Institutional Review Board (IRB) of the Institute of Basic Medical Sciences, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences, Beijing, China (015-2015) and informed consent from all participants/legal guardians of children under 18, peripheral blood samples were collected from all available family members of AR-OI patients. <sentence_start/>Skin samples were collected from some of the patients based on the availability.

Clinical parameters of probands were recorded at their first visit, including age, gender, height, times of fractures, presence of ptosis, scoliosis, blue sclerae, dentinogenesis imperfecta, and ability of walking. <sentence_start/>Height was also converted to Z-score calculated based on the age and medium height of Chinese population (<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.23718" pmid="30715774" count="1">Li et al., 2019</citation>).
Variant Nomenclature

Variants were named according to the nomenclature provided by Human Genome Variation Society<sup>1</sup>. <sentence_start/>Genomic DNA and cDNA sequences of <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic> ( ), <italic toggle="yes">CRTAP</italic> ( ), <italic toggle="yes">SERPINH1</italic> ( ), <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic> ( ), <italic toggle="yes">PLOD2</italic> ( ), <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> ( ), <italic toggle="yes">SEC24D</italic> ( ), <italic toggle="yes">P3H1</italic> ( ) were obtained from National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) reference sequence and University of California, Santa Cruz (UCSC) Genome browser database<sup>2</sup>.
Whole Exome Sequencing (WES)

Samples from 59 probands underwent WES process. <sentence_start/>Genomic DNA was extracted from leukocytes using a standard sodium dodecyl sulfate-proteinase <sc>K</sc>-phenol/chloroform extraction method. <sentence_start/>1-3 μg genomic DNA was used for WES as described previously (<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.23718" pmid="30715774" count="1">Li et al., 2019</citation>). <sentence_start/>DNA was fragmented as 150 bp, and the primers and adapters were then ligated to the DNA fragments to construct libraries. <sentence_start/>The analysis was performed on singletons, looking on previously known genes as filtering criteria. <sentence_start/>Sequencing was carried out on HiSeq 4000 System (Illumina). <sentence_start/>SAMtools mpileup and bcftools were used for variant calling and SNP/Indels identification. <sentence_start/>Control-FREEC was utilized for CNV detection.
Genomic Panel Sequencing

Fifteen probands were examined by genomic panel sequencing. <sentence_start/>Customized panel sequencing including 184 genes related to the monogenic disorders focused in our lab was conducted as described previously (<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.23718" pmid="30715774" count="1">Li et al., 2019</citation>). <sentence_start/>21 OI-related genes were included with 18 recessive OI genes. <sentence_start/>Sequencing was performed on the HiSeq 2500 System (Illumina, San Diego, CA, United States). <sentence_start/>All reference sequences were based on the GRCh37/hg19 assembly of the human genome.
Confirmation of Pathogenic Mutation by Sanger Sequencing

To verify the candidate mutations detected by WES or Panel Sequencing, genomic DNA was amplified following the PCR program: 95°C for 3 min; 94°C for 30 s, 58°C for 30 s, 72°C for 50 s (35 cycles); 72°C for 8 min. <sentence_start/>PCR amplified fragments was subjected to Sanger Sequencing based on Applied Biosystems 3730xl DNA Analyzer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, United States). <sentence_start/>Sequence was analyzed using CodonCode Aligner (version 6.0.2.6; CodonCode, Centerville, MA, United States).
Isolation and Culturing of Dermal Fibroblasts

To test the splicing effect caused by two variants in <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic> in proband PUMC-121 on endogenous level, skin samples of the proband and an ethnically matched healthy individual were collected from fresh skin biopsies. <sentence_start/>Human fibroblasts were maintained at 37°C and 5% CO<sub>2</sub> and supplied with F-12 supplemented with 1% <sc>L</sc>-glutamine, 20% fetal bovine serum, 1% sodium pyruvate, and 1% penicillin-streptomycin.
RNA Level Analysis

When a mutation was located in an intron, RNA level analysis would be conducted. <sentence_start/>Total RNA was isolated from peripheral blood or skin fibroblasts using Trizol reagent (Invitrogen, Cat. <sentence_start/>No. 15596018) followed by cDNA preparation using GoScript<sup>TM</sup> Reverse Transcription System (Promega, Cat. <sentence_start/>No. A5001), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. <sentence_start/>cDNA was used for sequencing or for quantitative PCR analysis.
Quantitative PCR (qPCR)

qPCR was carried out to detect large fragment deletion and mRNA expression level of <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic> gene. <sentence_start/>PCR amplification was carried out with SYBR Premix ExTaq (Takara, Bio., Dalian, China) and primer pairs (Supplementary Table S1) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. <sentence_start/>The reactions were monitored continuously in a Rotor-Gene 6000 instrument (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) according to the following program: 95°C for 3 min followed by 40 cycles of 95°C for 10 s, 60°C for 15 s, and 72°C for 20 s. <sentence_start/>The relative copy number (RCN) of the targeted sequence was normalized to the expression levels of GAPDH by calculating the ΔCt (Ct<sub>gene of interest</sub> - Ct<sub>GAPDH</sub>), and RCN = 2<sup>-ΔΔCt</sup>.
T-Clone Sequencing

T-Clone sequencing was used when Sanger sequencing results showed interlaced alleles. <sentence_start/>Briefly, The PCR product of target samples with disrupted signals was linked to the pMD19-T vector. <sentence_start/>The ligation reaction contained 4 μl Solution I (Takara, Shiga, Japan), 1 μl pMD19-T vector and 5 μl purified PCR product. <sentence_start/>DNA Sanger sequencing was performed followed by vector ligation, <italic toggle="yes">E. coli</italic> transformation and bacterial culturing.
Statistical Analysis

Statistical analysis was conducted for age of first onset, times of fractures, frequency of fractures, height, height Z-score and ptosis for the patients with pathogenic genes <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic>. <sentence_start/>GraphPad Prism (version 6.00; GraphPad Software, La Jolla, CA, United States) was used for statistical analysis and was performed for <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> ≥ 9. <sentence_start/>Differences between three or more groups were analyzed by one-way ANOVA, and comparisons between two groups were analyzed by student <italic toggle="yes">t</italic>-test. <sentence_start/>Graphs were presented as average ± standard deviation, and <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.05 was considered as significant difference.
Results
Phenotypic Characterization of AR-OI

We recruited 74 probands (39 males, 34 females, and one gender unknown fetus) with AR-OI from 60 non-consanguineous families and 14 consanguineous families. <sentence_start/>Except for the fetus, their ages ranged from 6 months to 35 years old and their parents were confirmed to be unaffected. <sentence_start/>The clinical manifestations of the 74 probands, including frequent fractures, scoliosis, short stature, blue sclerae, ptosis, disability to walk and dentinogenesis imperfecta (DI) were recorded and analyzed (Figure 1). <sentence_start/>Phenotypes of all probands were summarized in Supplementary Table S2. <sentence_start/>These patients presented severe phenotypes: most of them showed disability to walk (72.86%, Figure 1C) and scoliosis (65.28%, Figure 1D). <sentence_start/>Nearly half of them experienced more than 2 fracture times per year (54.05%, Figure 1F), 38.03% of them had dentinogenesis imperfecta (Figure 1B), and 38.03% of patients presented extremely low short statures with a Z score less than −4 SD (corresponding to type III OI). <sentence_start/>Compared to dominant inherited OI, blue sclerae was less frequent (32.43%) in AR-OI individuals. <sentence_start/>A unique phenotype, ptosis (23.88%), was observed in recessive inherited OI patients (Figure 1A), but was absent in dominant OI patients. <sentence_start/>None of AR-OI individuals displayed hearing loss or intellectual disability.
FIGURE 1

Phenotypic characteristics of AR-OI patients <bold>(A-F)</bold>. <sentence_start/>AR-OI patients had severe clinical manifestations including ptosis <bold>(A)</bold>, dentinogenesis imperfecta <bold>(B)</bold>, severe limb deformity and disability to walk independently <bold>(C)</bold>, scoliosis <bold>(D)</bold>, skeleton deformity <bold>(E)</bold>, and frequent fractures <bold>(F)</bold>. <sentence_start/><bold>(G)</bold> Percentage of the presence of each clinical manifestation in AR-OI probands.
Genotypic Characterization of Recessive OI
Variants Identification of Recessive OI

Variants of the 74 probands were identified in <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 30), <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 22), <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 10), <italic toggle="yes">SERPINH1</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 2), <italic toggle="yes">CRTAP</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3), <italic toggle="yes">PLOD2</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 1), <italic toggle="yes">P3H1</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3), and <italic toggle="yes">SEC24D</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3) (Table 1 and Figure 2B). <sentence_start/>Mutations in <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> showed the highest percentage (40.54%) in this cohort, followed by mutations in <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic> (29.73%) and <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic> (13.51%, Figure 2A).
FIGURE 2

Genotypic characterization of AR-OI patients. <sentence_start/><bold>(A)</bold> Mutation distribution in Chinese AR-OI patients. <sentence_start/><bold>(B)</bold> The number of pedigrees in each pathogenic gene. <sentence_start/><bold>(C)</bold> Distribution of mutation types in Chinese AR-OI patients.

Four major types of variants were found in this cohort, including missense, nonsense, frameshift and splicing mutations. <sentence_start/>We analyzed the number of each type of variant in each pathogenic gene and found that missense mutation was the main variant type in <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">SERPINH1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">SEC24D</italic>, and frameshift was frequently observed in <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic> (Figure 2C). <sentence_start/>Most variants were located at exons, but a homozygous intronic variant c.1153-3C > G was found in <italic toggle="yes">CRTAP</italic> (PUMC-456) (Supplementary Figure S1). <sentence_start/>Sequencing analysis of RT-PCR product of RNA isolated from dermal fibroblasts of this proband and his father confirmed that variant c.1153-3C > G led to an insertion of AG in the mutant transcript (Supplementary Figure S1C).
Establishment of Mutation Spectrums of <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic>

We identified 82 variants including 25 novel variants and 57 HGMD (professional 2020.01) reported variants (Table 1). <sentence_start/>Note that there were 36 variants reported in our previous study (<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.23718" pmid="30715774" count="1">Li et al., 2019</citation>). <sentence_start/>Because most variants are located in <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic>, the mutation spectrums of these genes were established (Figure 3).
FIGURE 3

Mutation spectrum of <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> <bold>(A)</bold>, <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic> <bold>(B)</bold>, and <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic> <bold>(C)</bold> of Chinese AR-OI patients. <sentence_start/>Black boxes represent the exons in each gene and lines represent the introns. <sentence_start/>Variants found in this study are listed above the boxes with novel variants in red and reported variants in black. <sentence_start/>Variants that have been reported previously are also listed under the boxes. <sentence_start/>Notation *digit indicates the number of probands carrying the same variant.
<italic toggle="yes">WNT</italic>1

We found 28 variants in <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> from 30 probands, including 21 reported variants and 7 novel variants (Table 1 and Figure 3A). <sentence_start/>There were some hotspot variants in <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic>: homozygous mutation c.506dupG(p.Cys170Leufs<sup>∗</sup>6) was found in three unrelated non-consanguineous families (PUMC-10, 21, and 221), leading to the production of truncated protein; Mutation c.677C > T(p.Ala133Thr) was observed in PUMC-3, 145, 247, 258, 471, and 554; Mutation c.620G > A (p.Arg207His) occurred in two probands (PUMC-128 and 329) and three non-consanguineous families (PUMC-217, 226, and 490), representing a hotspot in this Chinese cohort.
<italic toggle="yes">SERPINF</italic>1

Eight consanguineous and 14 non-consanguineous families were identified with mutations in <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic>, including 21 variants (14 reported variants and 7 novel variants) (Table 1 and Figure 3B). <sentence_start/>A known homozygous mutation, c.77dupC (p.Glu27Glyfs<sup>∗</sup>38), was found in three non-consanguineous families, which resulted in frameshift and truncated protein. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, there were three siblings from a consanguineous family (PUMC-527) identified with same homozygotes of a novel variant, c.907C > T in <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic>, but they exhibited extremely different phenotypes (Supplementary Figure S2). <sentence_start/>The proband had severe scoliosis and unable to walk independently with more than 45 times of fracture. <sentence_start/>However, his elder sister, harboring the same genotype, did not present any OI phenotype at all with only once fracture lifetime.
<italic toggle="yes">FKBP1</italic>0

Thirteen variants in <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic>, including 10 known variants and 3 novel variants, were identified in 10 non-consanguineous families (Table 1 and Figure 3C). <sentence_start/>Hotspot c.831indelC was identified in PUMC-157, 207, 431, 525 and 536, and these variants led to a premature termination codon. <sentence_start/>Hotspot c.344G > A was identified in PUMC-157, 405, and 431. <sentence_start/>Among the patients with variants in <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic>, three special cases needed to be highlighted. <sentence_start/>Case I, Patient PUMC-405 was a compound heterozygote with mutations in <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic>. <sentence_start/>Sanger sequencing analysis by software <italic toggle="yes">Chromas</italic> showed disrupted signals in exon 2 in <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic> (Supplementary Figure S4A), and two alleles were separated by T clone sequencing of the mutant region: c.320_353del(p.107_118del) with a 34 bp deletion (Supplementary Figure S4B), and a missense mutation c.344G > A(p.Arg115Gln) within the deleted region (Supplementary Figure S4C); Case II, Patient PUMC-207 harbored a gross deletion and an indel variant in <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic>. <sentence_start/>The compound mutations found in proband PUMC-207 were inherited from the parents: the indel of c.831delC was inherited from the mother and the gross deletion of chr17: g.39974881_39980318del (hg19) was inherited from the father, which was confirmed in breakpoint analysis using Gap-PCR and Sanger sequencing (Supplementary Figure S5); Case III, Patient PUMC-121 was previously reported that an intronic variant c.918-6T > G and a variant in adjacent exon c.1016G > A in <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic> similarly drove to skipping of exon 6, indicated by a minigene assay (Supplementary Figures S6A,B) (<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.23718" pmid="30715774" count="1">Li et al., 2019</citation>). <sentence_start/>Based on the sequencing results from cDNA (Supplementary Figure S6C) and RNA isolated from the patient’s dermal fibroblasts in the follow up study, we found that variant c.918-6T > G caused skipping of exon 6 and variant c.1016G > A caused partial skipping of exon 6. <sentence_start/>This was confirmed by qPCR analysis (Supplementary Figure S6D).
Correlation Between Genotypic and Phenotypic Changes

In order to answer whether there is a correlation between genotypes and observed phenotypes in AR-OI patients, we first analyzed the sites of fractures in patients harboring different pathogenic genes. <sentence_start/>We did not find significant difference in fracture locations among patients with different causative genes (Figure 4A). <sentence_start/>We then analyzed the phenotypes including fracture times, scoliosis, height, blue sclerae, DI, walking ability, and ptosis in these patients. <sentence_start/>Statistical analysis was conducted for <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic>, with > 3 probands (Supplementary Table S3), and only ptosis was significantly different between groups.
FIGURE 4

Correlation analysis of genotype and phenotype of Chinese AR-OI patients. <sentence_start/><bold>(A)</bold> Analysis of fracture sites in patients with variants in <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">SERPINH1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">CRTAP</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PLOD2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">P3H1</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">SEC24D</italic>. <bold>(B)</bold>. <sentence_start/>Fracture frequencies in patients with and without ptosis phenotype. <sentence_start/>Comparison of age of first onset <bold>(C)</bold> and height <bold>(D)</bold> of patients with variants in <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic> (*<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.05, **<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.01).
Patients With <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> Mutation Had Ptosis Phenotype

We noticed that AR-OI patients carrying <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> mutations were prone to developing ptosis, with 46.67% penetrance (Supplementary Table S3). <sentence_start/>This manifestation was common in patients with a homozygous function loss of <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic>, but was rare in patients with a loss of <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic>. <sentence_start/>Ptosis distribution displayed significant difference in different genes (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.0042). <sentence_start/>In patients with <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> mutations, those with ptosis also showed more severe skeletal dysfunctions including higher fracture frequency (Figure 4B) and unable to walk independently (80%), as compared to those without ptosis.
Patients With Variants in <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic> Presented a Distinct Phenotype

Compared to patients with mutations in <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic>, patients with variants in <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic> showed significantly delayed first fracture age (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.0072, Figure 4C) and taller height (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.0460, Figure 4D).
Discussion

With the development of next generation sequencing, genes associated with OI have been well-studied and identified. <sentence_start/>We examined mutation spectrum of AR-OI in a large cohort of 74 Chinese OI families. <sentence_start/>Current study unraveled 25 novel variants from 82 identified variants, and demonstrated <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> mutation as the most frequent mutation in all AR-OI genes. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, these AR-OI patients showed a unique phenotype, ptosis.

Type I collagen is a heterotrimer structure with two alpha 1 chains and one alpha 2 chain. <sentence_start/>Dominant OI is caused by mutations in <italic toggle="yes">COL1A1</italic> or <italic toggle="yes">COL1A2</italic>, and phenotypes can vary from mild to moderate/severe depending on the whether the collagen defect was caused by haplo-insufficiency or helical mutations that led to dominant negative effect (<citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1359/jbmr.091109" pmid="19929435" count="1">Rauch et al., 2010</citation>; <citation rid="B15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ejhg.2015.81" pmid="25944380" pmcid="PMC4795106" count="1">Lindahl et al., 2015</citation>). <sentence_start/>In AR-OI, alteration occurs during post translational modification progress when a triple helix pro-collagen is already formed, and hence most of these mutations affect both the synthesis of the whole type I collagen protein and bone homeostasis. <sentence_start/>Accordingly, AR-OI patients often exhibit more severe phenotypes than dominant OI, including significantly earlier first fracture age, higher fracture frequency, higher percentage of scoliosis and higher proportion of disability to walk (<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.23718" pmid="30715774" count="1">Li et al., 2019</citation>). <sentence_start/>Consistent with previous findings, more severe clinical manifestations were also observed in a cohort of Chinese patients with recessive OI in current study, including a high rate of scoliosis, disability of independent walking, extreme short stature, and high facture frequency (Figure 1G).

Current study in Chinese AR-OI patients suggests that <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> is the most frequently involved gene, followed by <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic>. <sentence_start/>These findings differ from that in Caucasian population, which showed that <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic> was the highest, followed by <italic toggle="yes">CRTAP</italic> (<citation rid="B4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00198-016-3709-3701" pmid="27509835" count="1">Bardai et al., 2016</citation>). <sentence_start/>The most distinct phenotypic characteristic in Chinese AR-OI patients was a unique ptosis phenotype, which was presented almost exclusively in patients associated with <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> variants (Supplementary Table S3). <sentence_start/>This result is consistent with recent finding that ptosis was a hallmark for OI patients with <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> mutations from Indian and Turkish families (<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.61119" pmid="30896082" count="1">Nampoothiri et al., 2019</citation>), and that from seven Chinese families (<citation rid="B18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bone.2018.06.018" pmid="29935254" count="1">Lu et al., 2018</citation>). <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> signaling was critical for the cross talk between osteoblastic lineage and osteoclastic-lineage cells (<citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/NEJMoa1215458" pmid="23656646" pmcid="PMC3709450" count="1">Laine et al., 2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>In addition to its vital importance in bone homeostasis (<citation rid="B19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/scitranslmed.aau7137" pmid="30404864" count="1">Luther et al., 2018</citation>), <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> also plays an essential role in neurological development (<citation rid="B6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/jmedgenet-2013-101750" pmid="23709755" count="1">Faqeih et al., 2013</citation>; <citation rid="B2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/jmedgenet-2015-103476" pmid="26671912" pmcid="PMC4898782" count="1">Aldinger et al., 2016</citation>). <sentence_start/>Because patients displayed ptosis all suffered neurological dysfunctions (<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.61119" pmid="30896082" count="1">Nampoothiri et al., 2019</citation>), it was postulated that ptosis phenotype may be associated with impaired brain or nerve development. <sentence_start/>Although we did not observe any intellectual problem in AR-OI patients with ptosis phenotype, these patients developed more severe skeletal phenotypes than those without ptosis (Figure 4D). <sentence_start/>No correlation was found between ptosis and mutation type or variant location. <sentence_start/>The mechanism of the development of ptosis in patients with <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> variant-induced AR-OI remains to be elucidated in future studies.

The severity of skeletal phenotype was compared in patients with <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic> variants. <sentence_start/>Patients with variants in <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic> had the highest number of average fracture times (30.77 ± 6.626) and highest frequency of fractures (4.193 ± 0.7986 n/year). <sentence_start/>However, their stature is the tallest (108.7 ± 3.154 cm, Supplementary Table S3). <citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bone.2018.02.029" pmid="29499418" count="1">Mrosk et al. (2018)</citation> reported that the phenotypic severity of genes associated with OI is: <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> > <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic> > <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic>, based on findings from 50 OI families, including 24 recessive OI families. <sentence_start/>In the current study, patients with <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> variants presented the shortest height (97.40 ± 3.889) and highest percentage of scoliosis 80.00%, but did not show any significant difference in other parameters such as height Z-score, blue sclerae, dentinogenesis imperfecta and disability of independent walking from patients with variants in <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic> (Supplementary Table S3). <sentence_start/>It needs to be noted that patients with <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic> variants all presented a short neck phenotype and severe spinal malformation (Supplementary Figure S3). <sentence_start/>FKBP10 is known to function as a molecular chaperone that interacts with collagen (<citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.M802535200" pmid="18786928" count="1">Ishikawa et al., 2008</citation>), but how it affects the cervical vertebra development remains unclear.

Recurrent variants were found in <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> (c.506dupG, c.677C > T, and c.620G > A), <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic> (c.77dupC, c.907C > T) and <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic> (c.831indelC and c.344G > A). <sentence_start/>All the homozygous of these recurrent variants corresponded to a severe phenotype (Supplementary Table S2). <sentence_start/>In particularly, OI patients with the novel variant c.907C > T in <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic> presented the most severe phenotypes: with 45-100 times of fractures, severe scoliosis and extremely short stature (Z-score < −8) (Supplementary Table S2). <sentence_start/>Previous studies also identified some recurrent variants, such as c.506dupG in <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic>, but did not find a clear correlation with the severity of phenotype (<citation rid="B17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cca.2016.07.012" pmid="27450065" count="1">Liu et al., 2016</citation>). <sentence_start/>Variant c.506dupG in <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> was found to be a hotspot region in 5 families among 10 total families examined (<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.61119" pmid="30896082" count="1">Nampoothiri et al., 2019</citation>). <citation rid="B10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jbmr.250" pmid="20839288" pmcid="PMC3179293" count="1">Kelley et al. (2011)</citation> reported the recurrent variant, c.344G > A in <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic> from a Caucasian child, who presented multiple fractures and a short stature. <sentence_start/>Further studies are needed to establish a causal-relationship between hotspot variant sites and phenotypes in these patients.

Frameshift occupied a high proportion in <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic> mutations (Figure 2C), suggesting that the two genes may have a distinct mechanism for OI development. <sentence_start/>In particular, most of variants located in <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic> may be involved in occurrence of nonsense/frameshift mediated pre-termination codon (Table 1), and these patients had very severe skeletal phenotypes, which is in line with previous findings (<citation rid="B5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2011.01.015" pmid="21353196" pmcid="PMC3059418" count="1">Becker et al., 2011</citation>). <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic> encodes pigment epithelium-derived factor (PEDF), which can inhibit osteoclastogensis by regulating osteoprotegerin expression (<citation rid="B1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bbrc.2009.11.139" pmid="19945427" count="1">Akiyama et al., 2010</citation>) and enhancing pre-osteoblast differentiation (<citation rid="B29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/emboj/cdg635" pmid="14657036" pmcid="PMC291830" count="1">Toru Akiyama et al., 2003</citation>). <sentence_start/>The truncated PEDF protein which mainly results in the absence of C terminal of PEDF, led to the malfunction of protein (<citation rid="B28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1046/j.1432-1033.2003.03374.x" pmid="12603315" count="1">Shao et al., 2003</citation>). <sentence_start/>Therefore, nonsense/frameshift mutations in <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic> may lead to truncated PEDF and severe OI phenotype.

In summary, we examined the largest cohort (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 74) of Chinese AR-OI probands and established the mutation spectrum of the three most frequent pathogenic genes (<italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">SERPINF1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">FKBP10</italic>) in this population. <sentence_start/>We also identified 25 novel variants and 7 hotspot variants. <sentence_start/>Genotypic and phenotypic analysis unraveled ptosis as a unique phenotype in patients with <italic toggle="yes">WNT1</italic> variants. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, patients with ptosis or hotspot variants showed more severe skeletal phenotypes than others. <sentence_start/>Current findings may enrich our understanding of the genetic basis of AR-OI, and our study provides new knowledge for a precise diagnosis of this disease in Chinese population.
